questions.question: Which is the most powerful system-defined role in Snowflake?
questions.explanation: C is correct. ACCOUNTADMIN is the top-level role that encapsulates both SYSADMIN and SECURITYADMIN. It should be used with caution and granted to as few users as possible. SYSADMIN manages objects, SECURITYADMIN manages grants, and USERADMIN manages users and roles.

questions.question: Which system-defined role is recommended for creating databases, schemas, and other objects?
questions.explanation: B is correct. SYSADMIN is the recommended role for creating and managing database objects like databases, schemas, tables, and warehouses. Using ACCOUNTADMIN for day-to-day object creation is considered a bad practice because of its elevated privileges.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the SECURITYADMIN role?

options.text: To create and manage databases and warehouses
To manage users, roles, and grant/revoke privileges
To monitor account billing and resource usage
To configure network policies and encryption keys

questions.explanation: B is correct. SECURITYADMIN manages users, roles, and privileges (GRANT/REVOKE). It inherits the USERADMIN role. Object creation is handled by SYSADMIN. Billing is managed by ACCOUNTADMIN. While SECURITYADMIN can manage network policies, its primary purpose is role and privilege management.

questions.question: Which access control model does Snowflake primarily use?

options.text: Discretionary Access Control (DAC) combined with Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Snowflake uses a combination of DAC (object owners can grant access to their objects) and RBAC (privileges are assigned to roles, which are then assigned to users). This provides a flexible and secure access control framework.

questions.question: In Snowflake's RBAC model, which statement is true about privilege inheritance?

options.text: Privileges flow from child roles up to parent roles in the role hierarchy
Privileges flow from parent roles down to child roles
There is no privilege inheritance; each role is independent
Only ACCOUNTADMIN inherits privileges from other roles

questions.explanation: A is correct. In Snowflake's role hierarchy, privileges flow upward — parent roles inherit all privileges from their child roles. For example, SYSADMIN inherits all privileges from custom roles that are granted to it. This is why best practice recommends granting custom roles to SYSADMIN.

questions.question: What happens if you create a custom role but do NOT grant it to SYSADMIN?

options.text: The role cannot be used by any user
SYSADMIN will not be able to manage objects owned by that custom role
The role is automatically deleted after 24 hours
ACCOUNTADMIN loses visibility into that role's objects

questions.explanation: B is correct. If a custom role is not in the SYSADMIN hierarchy, SYSADMIN cannot manage objects owned by that role. This creates 'orphaned' privileges. Best practice is to always grant custom roles to SYSADMIN so that SYSADMIN can manage all objects in the account.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the PUBLIC role in Snowflake?

options.text: A role that provides public internet access to Snowflake resources
A role automatically granted to every user; serves as the default minimum privilege level
A role for external users who access data through Data Sharing
A role that cannot be modified or have privileges granted to it

questions.explanation: B is correct. The PUBLIC role is automatically granted to every user in the account. Any privileges granted to PUBLIC are available to all users. It serves as the default minimum privilege level.

questions.question: Which Snowflake feature restricts access to an account based on IP addresses?
questions.explanation: B is correct. Network Policies allow you to create allowed and blocked IP address lists to control which IP addresses can access the Snowflake account. MFA adds an authentication factor. Row Access Policies and Column-level Security control data access, not account access.

questions.question: How does Snowflake's Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) work?

options.text: It is enabled by default for all users and cannot be disabled
It requires hardware security tokens for all users
It is powered by the Duo Mobile app and can be enrolled by individual users
It only works with federated authentication (SSO)

questions.explanation: C is correct. Snowflake MFA is powered by the Duo Mobile service. Individual users enroll themselves through the Snowflake web interface. It is not enabled by default and does not require hardware tokens. Administrators can enforce MFA via account or user-level settings.

questions.question: Which authentication method uses a public/private key pair instead of a password?
questions.explanation: B is correct. Key-Pair Authentication uses an RSA key pair (public key stored in Snowflake, private key kept by the user) for authentication instead of username/password. This is commonly used for service accounts and programmatic access. Federated Authentication and SAML are related to SSO.

questions.question: What is Federated Authentication in Snowflake?

options.text: Authentication shared between multiple Snowflake accounts
Single Sign-On (SSO) integration with an external identity provider using SAML 2.0
A method of sharing credentials between Snowflake and cloud provider consoles

questions.explanation: B is correct. Federated Authentication in Snowflake enables Single Sign-On (SSO) by integrating with external identity providers (such as Okta, Azure AD, or ADFS) using the SAML 2.0 protocol. This allows users to authenticate using their organization's credentials.

questions.question: Which Snowflake feature allows you to mask sensitive data at query time based on the querying user's role?
questions.explanation: B is correct. Dynamic Data Masking allows you to define masking policies on columns that conditionally mask or expose data based on the role of the user executing the query. This is applied at query time without modifying the underlying data.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Row Access Policies in Snowflake?

options.text: To restrict which rows a user can see based on conditions tied to their role or attributes
To encrypt specific rows in a table
To limit the number of rows returned by a query for performance
To audit which rows have been accessed by each user

questions.explanation: A is correct. Row Access Policies allow you to control which rows in a table or view are visible to a particular user at query time. The policy evaluates conditions (often based on the user's role) and filters rows accordingly. This is different from column-level masking which hides column values.

questions.question: What encryption standard does Snowflake use for data at rest?
questions.explanation: B is correct. Snowflake encrypts all data at rest using AES-256 strong encryption. This encryption is always on and cannot be disabled. All editions of Snowflake include this encryption at no additional cost.

questions.question: What is Tri-Secret Secure in Snowflake?

options.text: A feature that combines a Snowflake-managed key, a cloud provider key, and a customer-managed key for encryption
A way to share secrets between three Snowflake accounts
Three levels of network security policies

questions.explanation: B is correct. Tri-Secret Secure is a Business Critical feature that provides a composite encryption key made up of three components: a Snowflake-managed key, a cloud provider-managed key, and a customer-managed key. All three are required to decrypt data, giving the customer ultimate control.

questions.question: Which Snowflake edition is required for Tri-Secret Secure (customer-managed encryption keys)?

options.text: Any edition with an add-on purchase

questions.explanation: C is correct. Tri-Secret Secure is available only on Business Critical edition and above (including VPS). It allows customers to maintain their own encryption keys in their cloud provider's key management service (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, or GCP KMS).

questions.question: Which privilege allows a user to create objects within a schema?

options.text: All of the above can allow object creation, depending on the object type

questions.explanation: D is correct. Object creation depends on specific privileges: CREATE TABLE, CREATE VIEW, etc. are individual creation privileges. OWNERSHIP provides full control including creation. USAGE alone doesn't allow creation but is needed to use the schema. The combination depends on the specific object type being created.

questions.question: What does the USERADMIN system role allow you to do?

options.text: Create and manage databases and warehouses
Create and manage users and roles
Configure network policies and security settings

questions.explanation: B is correct. USERADMIN is specifically designed to create and manage users and roles. It can CREATE USER and CREATE ROLE. It is inherited by SECURITYADMIN, which adds the ability to GRANT and REVOKE privileges.

questions.question: In Snowflake, who is the default owner of an object?

options.text: The user who created the object
The role that was active when the object was created

questions.explanation: B is correct. In Snowflake, objects are owned by the role that was active (in use) when the object was created, not the user. This is a key concept in Snowflake's role-based access control. Ownership can be transferred using GRANT OWNERSHIP.

questions.question: Which privilege is needed to execute queries on a virtual warehouse?
questions.explanation: B is correct. The USAGE privilege on a warehouse allows a role to execute queries using that warehouse. OPERATE allows starting/stopping/resizing the warehouse. MODIFY allows changing warehouse properties. EXECUTE is not a valid warehouse privilege.

questions.question: What does the OPERATE privilege on a virtual warehouse allow?

options.text: Start, stop, suspend, and resume the warehouse
Resize the warehouse and change properties

questions.explanation: B is correct. OPERATE allows starting, stopping (suspending), and resuming a warehouse. USAGE is for executing queries. MODIFY allows changing properties like size. DROP requires OWNERSHIP.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Object Tagging in Snowflake?

options.text: To add search keywords to tables for faster queries
To assign metadata tags to objects for governance, tracking, and classification
To link related objects across databases

questions.explanation: B is correct. Object Tagging allows you to attach key-value metadata tags to Snowflake objects (tables, columns, warehouses, etc.) for data governance, classification, billing tracking, and sensitive data identification.

questions.question: Which system-defined role should be used for managing account-level settings like resource monitors and billing?
questions.explanation: C is correct. ACCOUNTADMIN is the only system-defined role that can manage account-level settings such as resource monitors, billing information, and account parameters. It combines the capabilities of SYSADMIN and SECURITYADMIN plus account-level management.

questions.question: A network policy in Snowflake can include which types of IP lists? (Choose two)
questions.explanation: A and B are correct. A network policy contains an allowed list (IPs permitted to connect) and an optional blocked list (IPs explicitly denied). Blocked list entries take precedence over allowed list entries for overlapping ranges. Priority and Quarantine lists do not exist.

questions.question: Network policies in Snowflake can be applied at which levels? (Choose two)
questions.explanation: A and B are correct. Network policies can be applied at the account level (affecting all users) or at the individual user level (overriding account-level policy for that user). They cannot be applied at database or table level.

questions.question: Which TLS version does Snowflake require for encrypted connections?
questions.explanation: C is correct. Snowflake requires TLS 1.2 or higher for all client connections. Older protocols (TLS 1.0, 1.1, SSL 3.0) are not supported due to known security vulnerabilities.

questions.question: What happens when you revoke a privilege from a role that has been granted to multiple users?

options.text: Only the user who originally received the privilege loses it
All users who have that role lose the revoked privilege
The privilege is only revoked for future sessions
Users must re-login for the change to take effect

questions.explanation: B is correct. When a privilege is revoked from a role, all users who have that role immediately lose that privilege. Privilege changes are effective immediately for all current and future sessions — no re-login is required.

questions.question: Which of the following is a Snowflake best practice for the ACCOUNTADMIN role?

options.text: Use ACCOUNTADMIN as the default role for all administrators
Grant ACCOUNTADMIN to as few users as possible and always use MFA
Use ACCOUNTADMIN for all day-to-day object creation tasks
Grant ACCOUNTADMIN to all team leads for flexibility

questions.explanation: B is correct. Snowflake strongly recommends granting ACCOUNTADMIN to as few users as possible (at least 2 for redundancy), always enabling MFA for those users, and never using ACCOUNTADMIN as the default role. Day-to-day tasks should use lower-privilege roles like SYSADMIN.

questions.question: What is the ORGADMIN role used for?

options.text: Managing objects within a single account
Managing accounts within a Snowflake organization, including creating new accounts and enabling replication
Managing network policies across all accounts
Auditing user activities across all accounts

questions.explanation: B is correct. ORGADMIN is an organization-level role that manages accounts within a Snowflake Organization. It can create new accounts, view usage across all accounts, and enable replication between accounts. It does not manage objects within individual accounts.

questions.question: Which feature allows Snowflake to automatically rotate encryption keys?

options.text: Automatic Key Rotation (available in Enterprise edition)
Key Rotation is not supported in Snowflake

questions.explanation: C is correct. Snowflake supports Periodic Rekeying on Enterprise edition and above, which automatically re-encrypts data with new keys on a regular basis (default every 30 days). All editions rotate the key hierarchy, but periodic rekeying (re-encrypting the data itself) requires Enterprise+.

questions.question: Which SQL command is used to grant a role to a user?

options.text: GRANT ROLE role_name TO USER user_name
ASSIGN ROLE role_name TO USER user_name
ADD ROLE role_name FOR USER user_name

questions.explanation: B is correct. The GRANT ROLE command assigns a role to a user. The syntax is: GRANT ROLE role_name TO USER user_name. ALTER USER can change the default role but doesn't grant roles. ASSIGN ROLE and ADD ROLE are not valid Snowflake commands.

questions.question: What is a Secure View in Snowflake primarily used for?

options.text: Encrypting view definitions so they cannot be read
Hiding the view definition and preventing data exposure through query optimization tricks
Making views available to external users only

questions.explanation: B is correct. Secure Views hide the view definition (DDL) from unauthorized users and prevent data exposure through techniques like pushing user-defined functions into the view's WHERE clause. The Snowflake optimizer does not expose the underlying data through its optimizations for secure views.

questions.question: Which OAuth providers does Snowflake support for authentication? (Choose two)
questions.explanation: A and B are correct. Snowflake supports its own built-in Snowflake OAuth for simplified integration and External OAuth for integrating with any OAuth 2.0 compliant identity provider (like Azure AD, Okta, PingFederate, etc.).

questions.question: What is the default role assigned to a new user in Snowflake if no default role is specified?

options.text: No role is assigned; the user cannot login

questions.explanation: B is correct. If no default role is specified when creating a user, the PUBLIC role is used as the default. PUBLIC is automatically granted to every user and cannot be revoked. The administrator should set an appropriate default role for each user.

questions.question: Which statement about Snowflake's data classification feature is correct?

options.text: It manually tags columns with sensitivity labels
It automatically analyzes column data and metadata to identify and classify sensitive information like PII
It encrypts classified data with a stronger encryption algorithm
It deletes data classified as sensitive after 30 days

questions.explanation: B is correct. Snowflake's data classification feature automatically analyzes column content and metadata to detect and classify sensitive data such as personally identifiable information (PII), payment card data, and other sensitive categories. It then applies system tags that can be used for governance.

questions.question: Can a user in Snowflake have multiple roles active simultaneously?

options.text: No, a user can only have one active role at a time
Yes, by using the USE SECONDARY ROLES ALL command
Yes, but only ACCOUNTADMIN users can activate multiple roles
No, but they can switch between roles using USE ROLE

questions.explanation: B is correct. With secondary roles (USE SECONDARY ROLES ALL), a user can have their primary role plus all other granted roles active simultaneously. This allows queries to access objects from multiple roles without switching. Previously, only one role could be active at a time.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the GRANT OWNERSHIP command?

options.text: To grant a user access to the Snowflake account
To transfer ownership of an object from one role to another
To create a new role with owner-level privileges
To share ownership between two roles simultaneously

questions.explanation: B is correct. GRANT OWNERSHIP transfers ownership of a Snowflake object from its current owning role to another role. An object can only have one owner at a time. The new owner gains full control over the object, including the ability to drop it.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a valid Snowflake system-defined role?
questions.explanation: C is correct. DBADMIN is not a Snowflake system-defined role. The system-defined roles are: ORGADMIN, ACCOUNTADMIN, SECURITYADMIN, USERADMIN, SYSADMIN, and PUBLIC. DBADMIN is a common role name in other database systems but not a built-in Snowflake role.

questions.question: Which feature allows Snowflake administrators to audit all user login attempts?
questions.explanation: A is correct. The ACCOUNT_USAGE.LOGIN_HISTORY view in the shared SNOWFLAKE database provides a record of all login attempts (successful and failed) for the account, including details like the user, client IP, authentication method, and error messages.

questions.question: What is the recommended minimum number of users who should have the ACCOUNTADMIN role?
questions.explanation: B is correct. Snowflake recommends at least 2 users have ACCOUNTADMIN for redundancy (in case one user is unavailable), but no more than necessary. All ACCOUNTADMIN users should have MFA enabled and should not use ACCOUNTADMIN as their default role.

questions.question: Which Snowflake feature allows you to set password policies for users?
questions.explanation: B is correct. Password Policies in Snowflake allow administrators to enforce password complexity requirements including minimum length, required character types (uppercase, lowercase, digits, special characters), password age, and history.

questions.question: What does the MONITOR privilege on a warehouse allow?

options.text: View warehouse usage and resource monitoring stats

questions.explanation: A is correct. The MONITOR privilege allows viewing warehouse usage statistics, resource monitor alerts, and query history for that warehouse. USAGE is for executing queries, MODIFY for changing properties, and OWNERSHIP is needed to drop.

questions.question: What is a Session Policy in Snowflake?

options.text: A policy that limits the number of concurrent queries
A policy that controls session idle timeout and maximum session duration
A policy that restricts which databases a session can access
A policy that determines the default warehouse for a session

questions.explanation: B is correct. Session Policies allow administrators to control idle session timeout and maximum session duration. This helps enforce security best practices by automatically closing inactive or long-running sessions.

questions.question: In Snowflake's role hierarchy, which role does SECURITYADMIN inherit?
questions.explanation: B is correct. SECURITYADMIN inherits the USERADMIN role. This means SECURITYADMIN has all USERADMIN privileges (create/manage users and roles) plus the ability to manage any grant (GRANT/REVOKE) on any object in the account.

questions.question: What happens when a blocked IP address in a network policy overlaps with an allowed IP address?

options.text: Both lists cancel out and the IP is neither allowed nor blocked
An error is thrown when creating the policy

questions.explanation: B is correct. When an IP address appears in both the allowed and blocked lists, the blocked list takes priority. The blocked list is used to deny specific IPs within a broader allowed range.

questions.question: Which Snowflake feature provides automatic detection and classification of sensitive data in columns?
questions.explanation: B is correct. Data Classification automatically analyzes column content and metadata to classify sensitive data such as PII, email addresses, phone numbers, and payment card data. It applies system-defined tags (SEMANTIC_CATEGORY, PRIVACY_CATEGORY) to classified columns.

questions.question: Which command shows all privileges granted to a role?
questions.explanation: A is correct. SHOW GRANTS TO ROLE role_name displays all privileges that have been granted to the specified role. You can also use SHOW GRANTS ON object to see who has access to a specific object.

questions.question: What is the difference between SHOW GRANTS TO ROLE and SHOW GRANTS OF ROLE?

options.text: TO ROLE shows privileges granted to the role; OF ROLE shows which users and roles the role has been granted to
TO ROLE shows users; OF ROLE shows privileges
OF ROLE is not a valid command

questions.explanation: B is correct. SHOW GRANTS TO ROLE shows what privileges the role has (e.g., SELECT on a table). SHOW GRANTS OF ROLE shows who has been granted that role (e.g., which users or parent roles).

questions.question: Can you grant the same privilege on an object to multiple roles?

options.text: No, a privilege can only be granted to one role
Yes, the same privilege can be granted to multiple roles
Only if the roles are in the same hierarchy
Only ACCOUNTADMIN can grant the same privilege to multiple roles

questions.explanation: B is correct. The same privilege (e.g., SELECT on a table) can be granted to multiple roles independently. Each role maintains its own set of privileges, and there is no restriction on granting the same privilege to multiple roles.

questions.question: What is the FUTURE GRANTS feature used for?

options.text: Granting privileges on objects that will be created in the future within a database or schema
Scheduling privilege grants to take effect at a future date
Granting temporary privileges that expire automatically
Granting privileges to roles that will be created in the future

questions.explanation: A is correct. FUTURE GRANTS automatically apply specified privileges to new objects of a given type (e.g., tables, views) when they are created within a database or schema. This eliminates the need to manually grant privileges on every new object.

questions.question: What does the IMPORTED PRIVILEGES privilege allow on a shared database?

options.text: It allows creating new objects in the shared database
It grants access to all objects in a database created from a share
It allows modifying the data in shared tables
It allows re-sharing the data with other accounts

questions.explanation: B is correct. IMPORTED PRIVILEGES is a special privilege used on databases created from shares. Granting it to a role gives that role access to all objects in the shared database. It is the only way to grant access to shared database objects.

questions.question: What encryption does Snowflake use for data at rest and in transit?

options.text: AES-128 at rest, TLS 1.0 in transit
AES-256 at rest, TLS 1.2+ in transit
AES-256 at rest, no encryption in transit
RSA-2048 at rest and in transit

questions.explanation: B is correct. Snowflake encrypts data at rest using AES-256 and requires TLS 1.2 or higher for all data in transit. Both are always on and cannot be disabled. This applies to all editions.

questions.question: Which privilege allows a role to create new schemas within a database?
questions.explanation: B is correct. The CREATE SCHEMA privilege on a database allows a role to create new schemas within that database. USAGE only allows using the database. OWNERSHIP provides full control but is more than needed for just creating schemas.

questions.question: What is SCIM in Snowflake used for?

options.text: Automated user and group provisioning/deprovisioning from identity providers

questions.explanation: B is correct. SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management) allows automated provisioning and deprovisioning of users and groups from identity providers like Okta and Azure AD. This ensures Snowflake user accounts stay in sync with the organization's IdP.

questions.question: Which Snowflake role hierarchy order is correct from most to least privileged?

options.text: ACCOUNTADMIN → SECURITYADMIN (inherits USERADMIN) and SYSADMIN → PUBLIC

questions.explanation: C is correct. ACCOUNTADMIN is at the top, inheriting both SECURITYADMIN and SYSADMIN. SECURITYADMIN inherits USERADMIN. SYSADMIN is a separate branch from SECURITYADMIN under ACCOUNTADMIN. All roles inherit PUBLIC at the bottom.

questions.question: What is managed access in Snowflake schemas?

options.text: A schema where only the schema owner can grant privileges on objects, not individual object owners
A schema with automatic data masking
A schema that only ACCOUNTADMIN can access

questions.explanation: A is correct. In a managed access schema (created with WITH MANAGED ACCESS), only the schema owner (or a role with MANAGE GRANTS privilege) can grant privileges on objects within the schema. Object owners cannot grant access to their own objects, centralizing privilege management.

questions.question: What does the MANAGE GRANTS global privilege allow?

options.text: Allows granting and revoking privileges on any object, even without ownership

questions.explanation: B is correct. The MANAGE GRANTS privilege allows a role to grant or revoke privileges on any object in the account, regardless of who owns the object. SECURITYADMIN has this privilege by default.

questions.question: Which command creates a network policy in Snowflake?
questions.explanation: B is correct. CREATE NETWORK POLICY creates a new network policy with allowed and blocked IP lists. After creation, it must be applied using ALTER ACCOUNT SET NETWORK_POLICY (account level) or ALTER USER SET NETWORK_POLICY (user level).

questions.question: Can a Dynamic Data Masking policy be applied to multiple columns?

options.text: No, each policy can only be applied to one column
Yes, the same masking policy can be applied to multiple columns of the same data type
Only if the columns are in the same table
Only ACCOUNTADMIN can apply a policy to multiple columns

questions.explanation: B is correct. A masking policy can be reused across multiple columns, as long as the column data type matches the policy's input/output type. This promotes consistency and reduces the number of policies needed.

questions.question: What is the difference between Dynamic Data Masking and External Tokenization?

options.text: Dynamic masking transforms data at query time within Snowflake; external tokenization replaces data with tokens using an external service
External tokenization is faster than dynamic masking
Dynamic masking permanently changes the data; external tokenization is reversible

questions.explanation: B is correct. Dynamic Data Masking transforms data at query time (the underlying data is unchanged). External Tokenization uses an external tokenization service (via external functions) to replace sensitive data with tokens. Both use masking policies, but the mechanism differs.

questions.question: What is the purpose of ACCESS_HISTORY in Snowflake?

options.text: Tracking which tables and columns were accessed by queries for compliance and auditing

questions.explanation: A is correct. ACCESS_HISTORY (in ACCOUNT_USAGE) provides a record of which objects (tables, columns, stages) were read or written by each query. This supports compliance auditing, data governance, and understanding data lineage.

questions.question: Which type of masking policy returns NULL for unauthorized users?

options.text: A masking policy that uses CASE WHEN CURRENT_ROLE() IN (...) THEN val ELSE NULL END

questions.explanation: A is correct. A Dynamic Data Masking policy can use conditional logic based on CURRENT_ROLE() or IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION() to return the actual value for authorized roles and NULL (or a masked value like '***') for unauthorized roles.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION function?

options.text: Checks if a role exists in the account
Checks if a specified role is active in the current session (primary or secondary)
Checks if a role has been granted to the current user
Checks if a role is a system-defined role

questions.explanation: B is correct. IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION checks if a specified role is currently active in the session, including as a secondary role. It is commonly used in masking policies and row access policies for role-based access control.

questions.question: Which statement about Snowflake's key rotation is correct?

options.text: Key rotation must be performed manually
Snowflake automatically rotates the hierarchical key every 30 days on all editions
Key rotation is only available on VPS edition

questions.explanation: B is correct. Snowflake automatically rotates the hierarchical encryption keys approximately every 30 days on all editions. On Enterprise+, periodic rekeying also re-encrypts the data itself with new keys. No downtime is required.

questions.question: What privilege is required to create a masking policy?

options.text: CREATE MASKING POLICY on the schema

questions.explanation: A is correct. The CREATE MASKING POLICY privilege on a schema allows creating masking policies. To apply the policy to a column, the APPLY MASKING POLICY privilege is also needed. These are separate privileges to support separation of duties.

questions.question: Which system function returns the current user's active role?
questions.explanation: A is correct. CURRENT_ROLE() returns the name of the currently active (primary) role for the session. CURRENT_USER() returns the current user name. SESSION_ROLE() and ACTIVE_ROLE() are not valid Snowflake functions.

questions.question: Can Row Access Policies and Dynamic Data Masking policies be applied to the same table?

options.text: No, only one type of policy can be active per table
Yes, both can be applied to the same table simultaneously
Only if they reference different columns

questions.explanation: B is correct. Both Row Access Policies and Dynamic Data Masking policies can be applied to the same table simultaneously. Row Access Policies filter which rows are visible, while masking policies control how column values are displayed. They complement each other.

questions.question: What is the APPLY ROW ACCESS POLICY privilege used for?

options.text: Attaching or detaching a row access policy to/from a table or view
Viewing which row access policies exist
Executing queries on tables with row access policies

questions.explanation: B is correct. The APPLY ROW ACCESS POLICY privilege allows a role to attach or detach a row access policy to or from a table or view using ALTER TABLE ... ADD/DROP ROW ACCESS POLICY. This is separate from CREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY (for creating) and OWNERSHIP.

questions.question: What is AWS PrivateLink used for with Snowflake?

options.text: Creating a private connection between a VPC and Snowflake that does not traverse the public internet

questions.explanation: B is correct. AWS PrivateLink (and Azure Private Link) creates a private, secure connection between your cloud VPC/VNet and Snowflake. Traffic stays within the cloud provider's private network and never traverses the public internet. Requires Business Critical edition.

questions.question: Which Snowflake edition is required for AWS PrivateLink or Azure Private Link support?
questions.explanation: C is correct. AWS PrivateLink and Azure Private Link connectivity require Business Critical edition or higher. These features provide enhanced network security for organizations with strict compliance requirements.

questions.question: What happens if a user's default role is dropped?

options.text: The user's default role falls back to PUBLIC

questions.explanation: B is correct. If a user's default role is dropped or the user no longer has access to it, the default role falls back to PUBLIC when they log in. The user can still switch to other roles they have been granted.

questions.question: Which command is used to enable MFA for a user?

options.text: Users self-enroll in MFA through the Snowflake web interface
CREATE MFA POLICY FOR USER user_name

questions.explanation: B is correct. Users self-enroll in MFA through the Snowsight web interface by linking their Duo Mobile app. Administrators can enforce MFA enrollment using the MINS_TO_BYPASS_MFA parameter or authentication policies, but the actual enrollment is done by the user.

questions.question: What is a Tag-Based Masking Policy?

options.text: A masking policy that is automatically applied to all columns with a specific tag
A masking policy that uses tags in its conditional logic
A tag that contains masking rules
A policy that masks tag values

questions.explanation: A is correct. Tag-Based Masking allows you to associate a masking policy with a tag. When that tag is applied to a column, the masking policy is automatically enforced. This simplifies governance by applying consistent masking across all columns with the same classification.

questions.question: Can Snowflake integrate with external key management services (KMS)?

options.text: No, Snowflake only uses its own encryption keys
Yes, through Tri-Secret Secure on Business Critical+ which integrates with AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, or GCP KMS

questions.explanation: B is correct. Through Tri-Secret Secure (Business Critical+), customers can bring their own encryption key stored in their cloud provider's KMS (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, or GCP Cloud KMS). The composite key requires all three keys to decrypt data.

questions.question: What is the SNOWFLAKE.CORE.BUDGET object used for?

options.text: Setting compute credit budgets with alerts when spending approaches or exceeds limits

questions.explanation: A is correct. Budgets allow administrators to monitor and control credit spending. You can set up budgets at the account or specific object level, configure spending limits, and receive email notifications when spending approaches or exceeds the budget.

questions.question: Which Snowflake view provides information about all login attempts including failures?
questions.explanation: A is correct. LOGIN_HISTORY in ACCOUNT_USAGE records all login attempts (successful and failed) with details including user name, client IP, authentication method, error messages, and timestamp. It retains data for up to 365 days.

questions.question: What does the OWNERSHIP privilege on an object allow? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Full control over the object including the ability to drop it
Grant privileges on the object to other roles

questions.explanation: D is correct. OWNERSHIP provides complete control over an object: the ability to alter, drop, grant privileges to other roles, and manage all aspects of the object. Every securable object has exactly one owner role at any time.

questions.question: What is the WITH GRANT OPTION used for?

options.text: Allows the grantee role to further grant the same privilege to other roles
Grants the privilege with read-only access
Grants the privilege only during business hours

questions.explanation: A is correct. WITH GRANT OPTION allows the role receiving a privilege to grant that same privilege to other roles. Without this option, only the object owner or a role with MANAGE GRANTS can further grant the privilege.

questions.question: How can you enforce MFA for all users in an account?

options.text: Create an authentication policy requiring MFA and apply it at the account level
Use ALTER ACCOUNT SET MFA_REQUIRED = TRUE
MFA cannot be enforced; it is always voluntary
Enable it in the Snowflake Marketplace

questions.explanation: A is correct. Authentication policies can be created to require MFA and then applied at the account level or user level. This forces all users (or specific users) to enroll in MFA before they can log in.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the POLICY_REFERENCES function?

options.text: Lists all policies in a schema
Returns which objects a specific policy is attached to, or which policies are attached to a specific object

questions.explanation: B is correct. The POLICY_REFERENCES table function (in INFORMATION_SCHEMA) shows the relationship between policies and objects. You can query it by policy name (to see where it's applied) or by object name (to see which policies are attached to it).
